author: Ellen Goethel,
title: Where have all the seagulls gone on the Seacoast this summer? - NewsBreak
text:
By Ellen Goethel, ,
19 hours ago I try to go out to the Isles of Shoals on the New Hampshire coast at least once every spring.
This year we had a nice fishing trip and picnic in Gosport Harbor between Appledore, Smuttynose, and Star Island. It dawned on me that something was missing. While there were hundreds of terns flying overhead, I saw not one gull. Where were the gulls?
Normally, while eating, they would fly overhead, circling the boat in the water, waiting for scraps. Finally, after about half an hour, a lone herring gull swam up to the side of the boat and looked expectant.
This is when I started really looking for them. Normally their piercing call would be a constant reminder that we were out at sea. Not a sound. While cruising around the Shoals looking at harbor seals and gray seals, we saw only a handful of herring gulls and one or two black-backed gulls . What was going on?
More: Don’t think we have big sharks in the Gulf of Maine? Think again.
On the way back to shore, we stopped to fish for mackerel. With baskets of mackerel on the deck and many swimming away, we should have expected to be surrounded by air and sea by both herring gulls and black-backs. Not one did we see. It was eerily quiet.
When I returned to shore, I asked commercial fishermen about the lack of gulls, and everyone I spoke with said they’d seen very few. Usually when they unload their catch, a whole flock would follow the boat into shore and try to steal an occasional fish from the deck. Only a handful could be seen around the Yankee Fishermen’s Cooperative in Seabrook.
For most of May, June and well into July, you could drive along Ocean Boulevard in Hampton without spotting a single gull — crows outnumbered them by far. I reached out to the Cornell Lab of Ornithology , and staff there reported seeing typical gull numbers for Rockingham County this season, though their data collection hadn’t yet extended into July.
About a week ago, we finally started seeing a few herring gulls along the beachfront. But even now, you can go hours without spotting one — or hearing their call. So what’s going on?
Pete Tilton of Defiant Lobster in Hampton was down in Gloucester a couple of weeks ago and sent me a video of gulls swarming the fishing pier. Hmm. This is food for thought.
The gulls in our area nest and roost (sleep) on the Isles of Shoals. There has always been a huge colony of them out there. During nesting season, everyone must walk around the Shoals Marine Lab on Appledore and wave a large stick overhead to keep from being attacked by an adult gull protecting their nest.
Every summer my husband teaches a couple of courses out at the Shoals Marine Lab about fisheries for the University of New Hampshire. He came home in June and told me he didn’t see any gulls nesting. He saw a handful of them on the back side of the island, but he was wondering what was going on.
More: What to know about the sea stars of Hampton Beach and the Gulf of Maine
New Hampshire Audubon , on its website, states that the only nesting area for gulls left in New Hampshire is the Isle of Shoals. They say that the numbers of gulls have decreased since their peak in the '70s due to the closure of many of the open dumps in the area. While this is true, last summer there was a huge contingent of both herring and black-backed gulls throughout the Seacoast.
What happened last winter to cause this severe decline in numbers? Some of the fishermen believe Avian flu took its toll along with a severe winter. We haven’t had a cold, windy and snowy winter in quite a few years. I believe this has taken a real toll on the local population of gulls.
I know that they are the bane of beachgoers, tourists and locals alike. Anyone who’s parked along the Seacoast has returned to find gulls dropping urchins or clams onto their car to crack them open — and leaving plenty of mess behind. We must wash the gulls’ poop off the car daily, and boy does it stick!
These animals, both herring and black-backs, are very intelligent and excellent problem solvers. Anyone who watches gulls for any length of time can see this. They have learned to swoop in and scoop bags of snacks and even whole sandwiches right out of unwary beachgoers’ hands. I just barely missed being hit with a bag of chips last year as I walked on the sidewalk. It landed just next to me, and whoosh, a whole flock of gulls descended to eat the remains that had spilled out of the bag.
While this activity can be annoying at times, these birds help clean up the mess that humans leave behind. They are incredibly adaptable to human behavior. They watch us! I can only imagine what they are thinking about the waste we leave behind.
Recently, I have had reports of returning herring gulls. Not even close to the number we had last year, but they are showing up. Where there was always a flock of birds fighting over a piece of food that had spilled out on the ground, now there are one or two. Still, the black-backed gulls are not showing up. Whenever a species decreases dramatically, there is a shift in the entire ecosystem. It looks like the terns have taken over this year. I will be contacting Cornell again and will keep you posted.
Ellen Goethel is a marine biologist and the owner of Explore the Ocean World Oceanarium at 367 Ocean Blvd. at Hampton Beach.
This article originally appeared on Portsmouth Herald: Where have all the seagulls gone on the Seacoast this summer?
